fathers/gregory-the-great/roles/4: Organiser of the mission to the English
fathers/gregory-the-great/summary: Roman aristocrat turned monk and pope whose Pastoral Rule, Moralia on Job, Dialogues and letters shaped the spirituality, preaching and church government of the medieval West, and who sent the mission to the English in 596.
fathers/gregory-the-great/story:
Gregory was born around 540 into a senatorial Roman family with papal ancestors and grew up amid the devastation of Justinian’s Gothic war. By about 573 he was prefect of the city, but he soon turned his family house on the Caelian Hill into the monastery of St Andrew and gave his Sicilian estates to found six more. Pope Pelagius II ordained him deacon and sent him as apocrisiarius (envoy) to Constantinople (c. 579–586), where he began the Moralia on Job for the monks who accompanied him.

Elected pope in 590 during plague and Lombard invasion, Gregory reluctantly took up what he called the burden of ‘the ship of the church, battered by waves’. He organised grain supplies from the papal patrimonies, ransomed captives, negotiated with the Lombards when imperial authority failed, and administered estates from Sicily to Gaul. More than 850 of his letters survive in the Registrum, revealing an administrator of formidable energy. He styled himself servus servorum Dei, ‘servant of the servants of God’, and protested at John the Faster of Constantinople’s title ‘ecumenical patriarch’.

His writings made Augustine’s theology accessible to the early Middle Ages. The Pastoral Rule (591) — sent to bishops across the West and translated into English by King Alfred — taught that the art of arts is the government of souls and that the preacher must adapt his words to each kind of hearer. The Moralia read Job on literal, allegorical and moral levels and became a medieval encyclopaedia of the spiritual life; it gives the classic list of seven principal vices with pride as their root. The Dialogues (593–594), including the Life of Benedict, popularised Italian saints and miracles and offered the clearest early teaching on a purifying fire after death.

In 596 he dispatched Augustine, prior of St Andrew’s, with some forty monks to Kent; Augustine baptised King Æthelberht and became first archbishop of Canterbury. Gregory’s letter of 601 to Abbot Mellitus advised that pagan temples be purified and reused as churches and that feasts replace sacrifices — a famous case of deliberate cultural adaptation. His letters to Serenus of Marseille (599–600) defended images as books for the illiterate while forbidding their worship.

Later tradition credited him with the codification of ‘Gregorian’ chant and of the Roman sacramentary; historians regard the chant attribution as a Carolingian legend, though he did make liturgical adjustments in Rome. In the East he is known as Gregory Dialogos, and the Byzantine Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts is traditionally attributed to him.
fathers/gregory-the-great/roots/0/text: Above all Augustine, whose teaching on grace, sin and contemplation he simplified and moralised; also Ambrose, Jerome and Cassian.
fathers/gregory-the-great/roots/1/text: A monk by choice, he made the contemplative life the measure of ministry and promoted Benedictine ideals through the Dialogues.
fathers/gregory-the-great/roots/2/text: His training as a Roman official shaped his careful administration of the papal patrimony and his juridical correspondence.
fathers/gregory-the-great/roots/3/text: Educated in grammar and rhetoric, though he affected disdain for classical polish and ‘would not bind the words of the heavenly oracle by the rules of Donatus’.
fathers/gregory-the-great/roots/4/text: His great works are commentaries on Job, Ezekiel, Kings and the Song of Songs, read through layered spiritual exegesis.
fathers/gregory-the-great/keyTeachings/0: Pastoral care as the ‘art of arts’: the pastor must balance contemplation and action and fit his teaching to each hearer.
fathers/gregory-the-great/keyTeachings/1: Scripture read on historical, allegorical and moral levels — ‘a river in which a lamb may wade and an elephant swim’.
fathers/gregory-the-great/keyTeachings/2: The seven principal vices, rooted in pride, as a map for self-examination.
fathers/gregory-the-great/keyTeachings/3: A purifying fire after death for light faults, and the value of the Mass offered for the dead.
fathers/gregory-the-great/keyTeachings/4: Images as instruction for the unlettered, not objects of adoration.
fathers/gregory-the-great/keyTeachings/5: Compunction and the desire for heaven as the heart of Christian life.
fathers/gregory-the-great/works/0/note: Handbook for bishops; translated into Greek in his lifetime and into Old English by Alfred the Great.
fathers/gregory-the-great/works/1/note: Thirty-five books of literal, allegorical and moral exegesis; begun in Constantinople.
fathers/gregory-the-great/works/2/note: Four books on Italian holy men; Book II is the Life of Benedict, Book IV discusses the soul after death.
fathers/gregory-the-great/works/3/note: Popular sermons that entered the medieval liturgical office.
fathers/gregory-the-great/works/4/note: Preached while the Lombards besieged Rome; contemplation and preaching.
fathers/gregory-the-great/works/5/note: Some 854 letters, including those to Mellitus (601) and Serenus (599–600).
fathers/gregory-the-great/doctrineContri: His Dialogues gave the early medieval West its most influential account of purgatorial fire and the efficacy of the Mass for the dead.
His pastoral theology defined the medieval ideal of the bishop as preacher and physician of souls.
Shaped Western teaching on contemplation, compunction and the mixed life of action and prayer.
His policy for the English mission set a pattern of gradual adaptation of pagan sites and customs.
His letters to Serenus became the standard Western defence of images as instruction.
fathers/gregory-the-great/laterInfluence: One of the four Latin Doctors; the Moralia and Pastoral Rule were among the most copied books of the Middle Ages, used by Bede, Isidore, Alcuin and Bernard.
Revered by the Anglo-Saxons as their apostle; the earliest Life of Gregory was written at Whitby c. 700.
Calvin regarded him as the last good bishop of Rome while criticising his teaching on purgatory and images.
Known as Gregory Dialogos; his Dialogues were translated into Greek by Pope Zacharias (c. 750).
His model of pastoral leadership is regularly invoked in Catholic, Anglican and Protestant pastoral theology.
fathers/gregory-the-great/reception/0/te: One of the four great Latin Doctors (proclaimed 1298); feast 3 September.
fathers/gregory-the-great/reception/1/te: Venerated as St Gregory Dialogos (12 March); the Presanctified Liturgy is attributed to him.
fathers/gregory-the-great/reception/2/te: Commemorated as the apostle of the English who sent Augustine to Canterbury.
fathers/gregory-the-great/reception/3/te: Admired as preacher and pastor; his purgatory teaching and the cult of relics he encouraged are rejected.
fathers/gregory-the-great/controversies/: His Dialogues’ miracle stories and purgatory teaching were attacked by Reformers as credulous; their authenticity was even challenged by Francis Clark (1987), though most scholars accept them.
The attribution of Gregorian chant to him is a later legend.
His letters endorse coercive measures against Donatists and pagans in some circumstances while forbidding forced baptism of Jews.
fathers/gregory-the-great/quote/text: Holy Scripture is like a river, shallow and deep, in which a lamb may wade and an elephant swim.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/summary: Bishop of Seville in Visigothic Spain whose Etymologies condensed classical and Christian learning into an encyclopaedia used throughout the Middle Ages, and who presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo (633).
fathers/isidore-of-seville/story:
Isidore was born around 560, probably in Seville, to a Hispano-Roman family that had fled Cartagena when the Byzantines occupied it. His elder brother Leander, bishop of Seville, educated him and played a leading part in the conversion of the Visigothic king Reccared from Arianism to Catholic Christianity at the Third Council of Toledo (589); his brother Fulgentius became bishop of Écija and his sister Florentina an abbess. Isidore succeeded Leander as bishop around 600 and held the see until his death in 636.

His episcopate coincided with the consolidation of a Catholic Visigothic kingdom, and Isidore aimed to give it a learned, unified church. He presided over the Second Council of Seville (619) and the Fourth Council of Toledo (633), which standardised the liturgy across Spain and Gaul, ordered cathedral schools for the training of clergy, and set out a theory of anointed kingship. The council’s canon 57 forbade forced conversion of Jews but required those already forcibly baptised under King Sisebut to remain Christian, an uneasy compromise reflecting Isidore’s own ambivalence.

His great work, the Etymologies (Etymologiae or Origines), arranged in twenty books by his friend Braulio of Zaragoza after his death, explains the world through the origins of words: grammar, rhetoric and dialectic, mathematics, medicine, law, chronology, God and the church, peoples, animals, geography, buildings, ships, food and tools. Drawing on Varro, Pliny, Servius, Augustine, Jerome and many lost compilations, it preserved classical knowledge for a world in which many sources were vanishing; more than a thousand medieval manuscripts survive.

He also wrote On the Nature of Things for King Sisebut, the Sententiae (a manual of doctrine and spiritual life drawn largely from Gregory the Great and Augustine), On Ecclesiastical Offices, a History of the Goths, Vandals and Sueves opening with the famous Praise of Spain, a world chronicle, On Famous Men, and the polemical On the Catholic Faith against the Jews.

Isidore’s authority later lent cover to the ninth-century Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, forgeries attributed to an ‘Isidore Mercator’ that strengthened papal and episcopal claims. Dante placed him among the wise in the Heaven of the Sun, and in 1722 Innocent XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/roots/0/text: The Etymologies begin with the liberal arts; Isidore’s method of explanation by word-origin comes from the grammatical tradition of Varro and Servius.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/roots/1/text: Book V of the Etymologies defines natural law, civil law and the law of nations from Roman jurists; Gratian’s Decretum opens with these definitions.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/roots/2/text: His theology largely compiles Augustine, Gregory the Great, Jerome and Cassian.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/roots/3/text: He developed the Visigothic ideal of a Catholic kingdom in which councils and anointed kings cooperate, building on Roman imperial models.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/roots/4/text: Transmitted summaries of Aristotelian logic (via Boethius and Cassiodorus) in Etymologies II.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/keyTeachings/: All learning, sacred and secular, serves understanding of Scripture and of God’s world.
The meaning of a thing can be grasped through the origin of its name.
Natural law is common to all peoples; laws must be just, possible and for the common good.
Kings rule justly only if they rule rightly (rex a recte agendo).
Prayer and reading as dialogue: in prayer we speak to God, in reading God speaks to us.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/works/0/note: Twenty-book encyclopaedia, completed and divided by Braulio after 636; the most-used reference work of the Middle Ages.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/works/1/note: Three books of doctrine and moral teaching, drawn largely from Gregory the Great.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/works/2/note: Explanation of the liturgy, feasts and orders of the church; key source for the Hispanic (Mozarabic) rite.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/works/3/note: Cosmology dedicated to King Sisebut, with diagrams of the world and seasons.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/works/4/title: History of the Goths, Vandals and Sueves
fathers/isidore-of-seville/works/4/note: Opens with the Laus Spaniae; a founding text of Spanish identity.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/works/5/title: On the Catholic Faith against the Jews
fathers/isidore-of-seville/works/5/note: Christological proof-texts against Judaism; influential in later anti-Jewish polemic.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/doctrineContr: Transmitted the liberal arts and patristic learning into the early medieval curriculum; mandated cathedral schools.
His On Ecclesiastical Offices and the Council of Toledo (633) standardised the Hispanic liturgy.
Shaped medieval ideas of Christian kingship, natural law and the cooperation of councils and kings.
His treatise against the Jews and the conciliar canons he oversaw shaped early medieval Christian policy toward Jews.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/laterInfluenc: The Etymologies were copied in almost every monastic library; Bede, Alcuin, Hrabanus Maurus and Vincent of Beauvais depended on them.
His legal definitions open Gratian’s Decretum; his name was attached to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals.
Regarded as the father of Spanish learning and a symbol of Visigothic Catholic identity.
Sometimes proposed as an informal patron saint of the internet for his encyclopaedic project.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/reception/0/t: Declared a Doctor of the Church by Innocent XIII in 1722; feast 4 April.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/reception/1/t: Venerated by many Orthodox as a pre-schism Western saint, especially in Western-rite communities.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/reception/2/t: Valued as a transmitter of classical and patristic learning; his anti-Jewish writings and support for Visigothic coercion are criticised.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/reception/3/t: Remembered for his role in the anti-Jewish legislation of Visigothic Spain, though he opposed Sisebut’s forced baptisms.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/controversies: His treatise against the Jews and the canons of Toledo IV contributed to Visigothic anti-Jewish policy.
Medieval forgers used his name for the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals.
Critics have dismissed him as a mere compiler; recent scholarship stresses his deliberate selection and arrangement.
fathers/isidore-of-seville/quote/text: When we pray, we speak with God; when we read, God speaks with us.
